citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC as required by the imported directional KL convention
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\rho)$ be a
metric space, where $\mathcal T$ is its Borel sigma-algebra. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sample space with a fixed sigma-finite
dominating measure. Suppose the supplied finite-valued densities
$(\theta,x)\mapsto p_\theta(x)$ and $x\mapsto p_0(x)$ are jointly measurable
and normalized relative to $\mu$, and observations are IID from $P_0$. Use
the directional convention for [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]:
$$K(\theta):=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta).$$
Assume $K^*:=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}K(\theta)<\infty$ and
$$\Theta^*:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)=K^*\}\ne\varnothing.$$
The set $\Theta^*$ is the **KL projection set** of the truth onto the model.
The **distance to the KL projection set** is
$$d(\theta,\Theta^*):=\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta^*}\rho(\theta,\vartheta).$$
A **relative KL neighborhood** of $\Theta^*$ of radius $\epsilon>0$ is
$$B_\epsilon:=\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta)-K^*\le\epsilon\}.$$

For any selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ with finite contrast, the relative
contrast on $B_\epsilon$ satisfies
$$K(\theta)-K^*=-\mathbb E_{P_0}\log\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}$$
whenever the displayed log ratio is integrable. This definition allows
$\Theta^*$ to contain multiple parameters and does not assert that the
posterior selects one of them.

Fix a selected $\theta^*\in\Theta^*$ as in
[[def-kl-projection-set-and-relative-kl-neighborhoods]]. Since its KL value is
finite, $p_{\theta^*}>0$ $P_0$-almost surely. For each $\theta\in\Theta$,
define the nonnegative set function
$$Q_\theta(A):=\int_A\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)}\,P_0(dx), \qquad A\in\mathcal A,$$
where the ratio is assigned value $0$ on the $P_0$-null set
$\{p_{\theta^*}=0\}$. Write
$$q_\theta:=Q_\theta(\mathsf X) =\mathbb E_{P_0}\left[\frac{p_\theta(X)}{p_{\theta^*}(X)}\right]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $q_\theta\ne1$, $Q_\theta$ is not a probability law. The local
sigma-finiteness lemma proves that it is a measure. The local product-measure
lemma then constructs $Q_\theta^n$ and proves its density relative to $P_0^n$
is $\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i)/p_{\theta^*}(X_i)$.

For a measurable test $\phi_n:\mathsf X^n\to[0,1]$,
once that product measure has been constructed,
$Q_\theta^n(1-\phi_n)$ means the nonnegative integral of $1-\phi_n$ under it.
It may be infinite; a hypothesis that this quantity tends to zero in
particular requires it to be finite for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

Under the setup of [[def-likelihood-tilted-measure-at-kl-projection]] and
[[lem-likelihood-tilted-measure-is-sigma-finite]], for each $\theta$ and
integer $n\ge1$, the sigma-finite product measure $Q_\theta^n$ exists and
has density
$$\prod_{i=1}^n r_\theta(x_i),\qquad r_\theta(x):=\frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\theta^*}(x)},$$
relative to $P_0^n$. Ratios are zero where $p_{\theta^*}=0$, as in the
likelihood-tilt definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta_1\ne\theta^*$ and put $r_1=p_{\theta_1}/p_{\theta^*}$ on $\{p_{\theta^*}>0\}$, with value zero on its $P_0$-null complement. The finite likelihood-ratio mean makes $r_1$ integrable. For $r_1\ge1$, [F11] gives $0\le\log r_1=\int_1^{r_1}u^{-1}du\le r_1-1\le r_1$, so the positive part is integrable. The log ratio is measurable by [F14]. Also $\mathbb E_{P_0}\log r_1 =-\bigl(K(\theta_1)-K^*\bigr)<0,$ by the extended relative-contrast hypothesis, with value $-\infty$ allowed.

For $t\downarrow0$, let $A(t)=\mathbb E_{P_0}r_1^t$. Since $r_1^t\le1+r_1$ for $0<t\le1$, [F8] gives $A(t)\to P_0(r_1>0)\le1$. If this limit is less than one, then $A(t)<1$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. If the limit equals one, split into $\{r_1\ge1\}$ and $\{0<r_1<1\}$. On the first set, $(r_1^t-1)/t\to\log r_1$ and, for fixed $t_0<1$ and $0<t\le t_0$, the mean-value theorem bounds this quotient above by $r_1^{t_0}\log r_1\le C r_1$ for a finite constant $C$: the function $r^{t_0-1}\log r$ is continuous on $[1,\infty)$ and tends to zero at infinity. On the second set, write $y=-\log r_1>0$. Then $(1-r_1^t)/t=y(1-e^{-yt})/(yt)$. The function $u\mapsto(1-e^{-u})/u$ decreases on $u>0$, since its derivative is $((u+1)e^{-u}-1)/u^2\le0$ by $e^u\ge1+u$: for $u\ge0$, $h(u)=\exp(u)-1-u$ has $h(0)=0$ by the exponential definition and $h'(u)=\exp(u)-1\ge0$ by the derivative formula and exponential monotonicity, the mean value theorem then gives $h(u)\ge0$. Hence the quotient increases to $y$ as $t\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence on the first set and monotone convergence [F9] on the second show $\frac{A(t)-1}{t}\longrightarrow \mathbb E_{P_0}\log r_1<0$ in the extended sense. Thus $A(t)<1$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$.

Choose such a $t$ with $s:=1-t$ in the left-neighborhood from the fractional-moment hypothesis. Then $M_s(\theta_1,\theta_1)=A(t)<1$. By continuity at $\theta_1$, there are an open neighborhood $G_{\theta_1}$ and $0<a_{\theta_1}<1$ such that $\sup_{\theta\in G_{\theta_1}}M_s(\theta_1,\theta)\le a_{\theta_1}$.

Define $\phi_{n,\theta_1} =\mathbf 1\left\{\prod_{i=1}^n r_1(X_i)>1\right\}.$ The score and test are measurable by [F10], [F14], and [F15]. On the rejection event the product raised to $t$ exceeds one. Repeated Tonelli integration under $P_0^n$ therefore gives $P_0^n\phi_{n,\theta_1} \le \left(\mathbb E_{P_0}r_1^t\right)^n =M_s(\theta_1,\theta_1)^n \le a_{\theta_1}^n.$ For the second error, let $g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}$ be the integrand defining $M_s(\theta_1,\theta)$, with the zero and infinite conventions in the Statement. On the $P_0$-full set where $p_{\theta^*}>0$, if $p_\theta>0$ and $p_{\theta_1}>0$ then algebra gives $g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}=r_\theta r_1^{-s}$; the displayed conventions extend this identity to the boundary values. On nonrejection, $\prod_i r_1(X_i)\le1$. If every factor is positive, this gives $\prod_i r_\theta(X_i) \le\prod_i\bigl(r_\theta(X_i)r_1(X_i)^{-s}\bigr) =\prod_i g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}(X_i).$ If some $r_\theta(X_i)=0$, both the density product and the right-hand product are zero under $0\cdot\infty=0$; if some $r_1(X_i)=0$ while every $r_\theta(X_i)>0$, the right-hand product is infinite and the inequality still holds. The product-density identity [F6] and repeated Tonelli [F7] now give, for $\theta\in G_{\theta_1}$, $Q_\theta^n(1-\phi_{n,\theta_1}) \le\left(\mathbb E_{P_0}g_{\theta,\theta_1,s}(X)\right)^n =M_s(\theta_1,\theta)^n \le a_{\theta_1}^n.$ The moment hypothesis makes these integrals finite on the chosen neighborhood.

Put $C_\eta=\{\theta:\rho(\theta,\theta^*)\ge\eta\}$. If $\rho(\theta,\theta^*)<\eta$, then every $\theta'$ with $\rho(\theta',\theta)<\eta-\rho(\theta,\theta^*)$ satisfies $\rho(\theta',\theta^*)<\eta$ by [F13]. Thus the complement of $C_\eta$ is open, so $C_\eta$ is closed by [F12]. By [F5], it is compact. For every point of $C_\eta$, step 3.1 supplies a neighborhood; [F4] gives a finite subcover $G_{\theta_1},\ldots,G_{\theta_k}$.

Set $\phi_n=\max_{1\le j\le k}\phi_{n,\theta_j}$. The union bound and step 4.1 give $P_0^n\phi_n\le\sum_{j=1}^k a_{\theta_j}^n,\qquad \sup_{\theta\in C_\eta}Q_\theta^n(1-\phi_n) \le\max_{1\le j\le k}a_{\theta_j}^n.$ Since the subcover is finite and each $a_{\theta_j}<1$, both bounds are at most $C_\eta e^{-c_\eta n}$ for suitable $c_\eta,C_\eta>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. The set $\{\rho(\theta,\theta^*)>\eta\}$ is contained in $C_\eta$, so the same type-II bound holds there. If $C_\eta=\varnothing$, the zero test has both errors zero.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 5.1 explicitly set phi_n=0 when C_eta={rho(theta,theta*)>=eta} is empty; its type-I error is zero and there are no type-II subjects.

Step 4.1 treats r_1=0 and r_theta=0 separately: a zero density product contributes zero, while a zero r_1 with all r_theta positive bounds the product by infinity; finite moment hypotheses control the integral.
Step 4.1 uses threshold product r_1>1, so equality belongs to nonrejection and the product-density inequality still holds. The finite cover can have one center with bound a_theta1^n.
Statement permits a singleton compact parameter space. For every eta>0 its separated set is empty, so the explicit zero-test branch supplies the required bounds.
Steps 2.1–3.1 choose 0<t<1 and s=1-t inside the assumed open interval; no endpoint fractional moment at s=1 or t=0 is substituted, and log mean -infinity is treated by monotone convergence.
Step 4.2 extracts finitely many neighborhoods from the compact separated set; step 5.1 takes the maximum of their tests and the separate empty-set branch avoids a maximum of no tests.

boundaries.reason: Statement asserts a sufficient compact unique-minimizer test construction under fractional-moment continuity, without claiming that exponential tests imply those hypotheses.
Statement explicitly disclaims generic testability on noncompact parameter spaces; it does not turn existence of tests into a characterization of compactness or uniqueness.

axioms.reason: A1 records the imported AC convention; no additional selection is made.
